cards.title: Service health and service state travel on separate paths
cards.atAShow: If Home Assistant or MPD is down when the engine starts, the lighting and music panels stay disabled all night. If MPD dies mid-show, the health row turns red alone while the music card keeps its playing look and the progress bar keeps moving. A volume change on one tablet's audio panel never reaches the other tablets' sliders.
cards.whyItHappens: Each venue service keeps two facts: its health in a central registry and its own state in its own record. The engine pushes the health row when health changes, and pushes a service's state only on a hand-written list of that service's events. An outage is on no list.
cards.designTerms: Each service module should own one record carrying health and state. Today the seam leaks: the broadcast module re-implements each service's change set as a per-domain event list, so the interface callers must know is the full event list, and locality is lost.

examples.text: Lighting panel stays unavailable all night if Home Assistant was down at engine start; nothing re-sends its state.
Music panel stays disabled if MPD was down at connect; the progress bar keeps moving after MPD dies.
A per-stream volume change on one tablet never reaches other tablets' sliders; the audio push list names no volume event.
Audio and lighting pushes rest on hand-listed events, so a missing event means a stale panel.

cards.seenLive: The owner reported the music panel not keeping up with live music; blue's review recorded the frozen lighting panel.

cards.title: Engine trusts its stale picture of outside programs
cards.atAShow: A video stayed stopped for about 28 seconds because the parser held each player message until the next one arrived. A false video finished can fire two seconds in, flipping the display back and restoring music. When MPD dies the engine still says playing and the controls stay dead until the next 15-second sweep. A cue with a 2-second video never completes.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine learns what VLC, MPD and the other programs are doing by parsing their text or event streams into a cached copy that starts from a default and carries no age. Re-reads are partial, and the video queue, cue timelines and health rows treat the copy as the program.
cards.designTerms: A reader module per outside program should own the engine's picture of it, behind one interface: read, stream, resync, last-read time. Today the parser, the player service and the queue are shallow: each exposes raw stream handling, so locality is spread across all three.

examples.text: Video stayed stopped about 28 seconds: the parser holds each message until the next header arrives.
A false video finished can fire two seconds in; display flips back, ducking restores, cues told video ended.
When MPD dies the engine's picture still says playing with the last track; only the health row goes out.
After an MPD crash the controls stay dead up to 20 seconds; the supervisor's restart is ignored.
A cue whose video ends before its first progress tick never completes and stays on screen.
The 15-second probe corrects the VLC picture but announces it on an event nothing hears for VLC.

cards.seenLive: Blue's worst live incident, the video that stayed stopped about 28 seconds, happened on the show machine.

cards.title: Engine and tests both assume they own the machine
cards.atAShow: On 2026-09-15 a unit test killed the live show's video player on blue's tree. In this tree the same run kills the live engine's VLC signal monitor and overwrites its process files. A killed engine leaves a full-screen player behind. Twenty-one test suites open a browser on the show TV. The operator's health script says VLC not found while the player runs.
cards.whyItHappens: The engine names and ends its helper programs by fixed file names and by command-line patterns over the whole machine, written as the only engine on the box. The test layers adopt whatever display, sound server and Bluetooth exist; that a layer is safe is claimed in comments, never checked.
cards.designTerms: A runtime-identity module should own which processes, files and windows belong to this engine instance. Today that seam does not exist: every service module and test harness names machine resources directly; the process supervisor is a shallow kill-by-pattern pass-through, so identity has no locality.

examples.text: A unit test killed the live video player on blue's tree; here it kills the signal monitor and overwrites process files.
Leftover cleanup looks for cvlc but the process is vlc, so a killed engine leaves a full-screen player.
Twenty-one suites start a real full-screen browser on the show TV pointed at the live port.
Starting any engine kills every pactl subscribe process of the user, including the live engine's sink monitor.
The health script says VLC not found while the player runs, because it looks for cvlc.
Fixing the reaper's name alone brings blue's unit-test kill back; the per-run process folder must land first.

cards.seenLive: A unit test killed the live video player on 2026-09-15; a kill guard logged the show box out on 2026-09-18.

cards.title: Several places answer the same question, each differently
cards.atAShow: Is a video playing has seven answers. A paused video counts as free, so a player is told their video was triggered while it waits, and releasing a held video plays over the paused one. Release All can stop at the first refused video. Music stays ducked after the queue is cleared. The downloaded report's two totals disagree.
cards.whyItHappens: Questions such as is a video playing, which teams exist and may the GM scan now are answered by several functions or stored values, each with its own rule and write path, so they disagree at the edges. No rule says which answerer every reader must use.
cards.designTerms: One resolver module per question should own the verdict. Today each reader, the queue, the command gate, the ducking engine, carries its own implementation of the same question, so the interface to the fact is as wide as its readers: shallow, no locality.

examples.text: Is a video playing has seven answers; a paused video counts as not playing for four of them.
Held cues and held videos live in two stores; Release All can stop at the first refused video.
Ducking keeps its own count of playing videos; music stays ducked after the queue is cleared.
The GM's permission to scan is read from a local copy; after a reload it blocks scans in an active game.
Which teams exist has several answers; a second GM adding the same name gets an error though the team exists.
The downloaded report has two different final totals per team: the timeline leaves out group bonuses, the standings include them.

cards.seenLive: The display's false healthy Check Now was reproduced in-process by the recovered review.
